newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysian youth leader apologises to Lee Kuan Yew. [CORRECTED 04:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Malaysian youth leader apologises to Lee Kuan Yew. [CORRECTED 04:15 GMT]

text.p: An outspoken Malaysian critic of Singapore has offered an apology to Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew over harsh remarks during a recent spat between the two neighbours, the Straits Times said on Friday.

The pro-government daily newspaper quoted Ahmad Zahid Hamidi as telling Singapore reporters: "If SM (Lee) is able to apologise...why not if I also express my apology to you people, especially to SM Lee personally?"
Zahid is the head of the youth wing of Malaysia's ruling United Malays National Organisation (UMNO).
UMNO Youth members were among the harshest critics of Lee over remarks he made in a court affidavit describing Malaysia's Johor Baru as a city "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Lee's comments, made in relation to a libel suit against an opposition politician, provoked fierce protest in Malaysia and a cooling in relations between the two countries.

Zahid's UMNO youth led an extraordinary demonstration in Johor Baru after Lee's remarks were publicised in March. The UMNO youth protesters shouted slogans and waved placards calling Lee "senile" and "ignorant".
Lee apologised twice for the remarks, and had them withdrawn from the legal record in the Singapore courts.
Zahid said on Thursday he wanted to "close the books" on the episode, the Straits Times said.

Asked about some of the specific slogans on placards during protests following Lee's remarks, Zahid said: "If you asked me personally, I shouldn't ask them to be writing like that. Personally, I do not agree...But things had happened. So as I told you, this is the real feeling of the people."
Zahid was in Singapore on Thursday to meet Information Minister George Yeo in the latter's capacity as leader of the Young PAP, the youth wing of Singapore's ruling People's Action Party.
Yeo welcomed Zahid's comments and call for closer relations between the two political youth wings, but said it would first require an environment which made it possible and natural.
Yeo said the two sides should maintain lines of communication. "If we don't talk, things can get worse than they need to be," he said.
Zahid was among three Malaysian leaders who made positive remarks on Thursday about relations with Singapore.
Minister of International Trade and Industry Rafidah Aziz told a news conference in Johor Baru that ties were back to normal, the national news agency Bernama reported.
"We are happy to extend co-operation," Rafidah said after meeting Singaporean officials to discuss a "growth triangle" involving southern Malaysia, northern Indonesia and Singapore.
"Singapore and Malaysia have been such close neighbours," she added.
Johor chief minister Abdul Ghani Othman, also at the press conference said: "There is no problem with the relationship."

The two nations are closely entwined by history, culture and business. They were united in the Malaysian Federation between 1963 and 1965 (corrects from "1993 and 1995") when Malaysia booted out its southern neighbour over basic policy differences.
